corruption vulnerabilities in regulated activities","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Regulatory hurdles in some sectors with critical forward linkages (e.g., foreign direct investment restrictions in surface, maritime and air transport) limit competition and, through the implications for input costs, harms the competitiveness of other sectors. Also, cumbersome licenses and permits procedures create vulnerabilities to corruption (e.g., road transport, custom brokerage and restaurants licenses, construction permits).","locator":"page 32","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Article IV Consultation, MAC-010","period_fit":"Assessment period 2022; persistent structural barriers","source_limitations":["Staff characterization of sector-level effects; specific affected sectors cited as examples rather than exhaustive enumeration"],"question_ids":["5B.4","5B.5"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0006","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico reversed key elements of the 2013 energy reform: a new electricity law replaced market auctions with non-market policies, concentrated regulatory power in CFE, disrupted existing contracts, and created conflicts of interest.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexico federal government; Parliament (Congress)","action":"enacted new electricity law replacing 2013 reform; rejected full constitutional reversal of 2013 reform","mechanism":"Parliament-approved new electricity law with non-market policies; regulatory power concentrated in CFE; contracts from 2013 reform disrupted","outcome":"policy uncertainty about energy sector direction; conflicts of interest; disrupted private contracts; reduced private sector participation in energy","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Actions to reverse the 2013 energy reforms remain incomplete, as Parliament rejected the change in the constitution needed for a full reversal, which has introduced policy uncertainty about the way forward. A new electricity law, however, was approved and has replaced auctions by nonmarket-based policies, with regulatory power given to the Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE), the state-owned electricity company. This has created conflicts of interest and disrupted contracts signed under the 2013 reform.","locator":"page 33","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Article IV Consultation, MAC-010","period_fit":"Post-2013 reform period; new law enacted prior to 2022 assessment; incomplete reversal and new law represent ongoing policy uncertainty","source_limitations":["Staff characterization of policy effects; contracts disrupted and conflicts of interest are staff assertions without quantified extent"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3","5B.4","5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0007","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's 2023 emission trading system pilot covers approximately 40 percent of emissions from a limited number of large entities, with no legally binding emissions caps and unclear scalability.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexico federal government","action":"expanded ETS in 2023 to pilot phase","mechanism":"pilot emission trading system covering large entities responsible for approximately 40 percent of emissions; auction system for allowances not yet introduced; no legally binding caps","outcome":"ETS market remains limited; ability to expand coverage is not clear; legally binding caps absent","dates":["2023"],"quantities":["approximately 40 percent of emissions covered (pilot phase)"],"excerpt":"Although these are responsible for around 40 percent of emissions, the ability to expand coverage is not clear.
